transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, doctor. Thank you. Well, I suppose the main thing, the reason I finally made this appointment, is that I barely sleep in any useful way anymore. I mean, I might physically be in bed, but it’s not actual rest. 

I’m an investment analyst, and lately, the moment my head hits the pillow, my brain just starts... spinning. I’ll just lie awake in the dark, obsessively replaying client models. I'll be running through spreadsheets in my head, second-guessing risk assessments, worrying about whether I factored in the right variables for a specific portfolio, just over and over. And then, if my body finally just gives out from sheer exhaustion, it doesn't even last. I inevitably wake up at 3 or maybe 4 in the morning, every single night, and I'm just wide awake. 

But it's this awful kind of awake, you know? My stomach is completely tight, just twisted up in knots, and I can't get back to sleep no matter what I try. I'll toss and turn, but my mind is already racing again. So I just lie there staring at the ceiling until it's time to get ready, and I go to work feeling like I never actually rested. I just sit at my desk feeling like I've already worked a full day before my shift even starts, and it's just becoming impossible to keep functioning like this.
Do you find yourself worrying excessively about things outside of work, like personal relationships, health, or other everyday matters, even when you're not thinking about your job?

You know, it's actually... no, not really. It's funny you ask that, because I was just thinking the other day about how little I actually care about anything else right now. I mean, my personal relationships are practically nonexistent at this point anyway. I just don't have the energy to maintain them, let alone worry about them. If a friend doesn't call me back, I don't sit there agonizing over whether they're mad at me or if I said something wrong, I just... I kind of just feel relieved that I don't have to try and carry on a conversation, to be honest. 

And as for my health, well, I suppose I probably *should* be worried about it, considering I'm 48 and my body feels like it's completely shutting down from this lack of sleep, but my brain just doesn't seem to have the capacity to care about it. It's like there's a strict limit on what my mind can process, and the firm just consumes every single drop of it. 

Even when I try to distract myself with everyday things—like, I'll go to the grocery store on a Sunday and try to just focus on picking out produce, just normal, mundane things—my mind doesn't latch onto whether the tomatoes are ripe or if I remembered to pay the electric bill or what I'm doing with my life. It just snaps right back to the risk models. It's always the models. So, no, the everyday stuff, the normal human concerns... they just don't even register on my radar anymore. I almost wish they did, because worrying about a water bill sounds like a vacation compared to this, but... no. It really is just the job.
Have you noticed a loss of pleasure or interest in activities that you used to enjoy, even things that used to make you feel good or relaxed?

Loss of pleasure? Um... no. No, I wouldn't say that at all, actually. I mean, I still like the same things I’ve always liked, and I still get the same feeling out of them. 

Like, I’ve always been an avid reader, mostly historical biographies—I actually just finished this massive, thousand-page book on the Romanovs last week, which was fascinating because the political dynamics are just so intricate, you know? And I still found myself completely absorbed in it. I still get that... that feeling of being totally engaged when I sit down with a good book and a cup of Earl Grey on a Sunday afternoon. 

And my garden, too. I have these incredible hydrangeas out back, the endless summer variety, and I still get a lot of satisfaction out of taking care of them. I was just out there this past weekend, testing the soil pH because I'm trying to get the blooms to turn that really deep, vibrant blue instead of the pinkish-purple they've been leaning toward lately. It takes a lot of aluminum sulfate to get the acidity right, and you have to be so incredibly careful not to burn the root system, but I still really care about getting it right. I still genuinely enjoy the whole process of it. 

I mean, sure, I’m physically exhausted while I’m doing these things because, like I was saying before, I’m running on maybe two or three hours of actual, fragmented sleep, so my body just feels like it's made of lead. I might have to sit down on the patio chair halfway through pruning the bushes just to catch my breath and rest my eyes for a second. But the actual interest? The enjoyment I get from seeing the flowers finally bloom or getting to the end of a really great chapter? That hasn't changed one bit. I still want to do those things. It's not like the color has drained out of my hobbies or anything like that. I just... I have to do them while I'm incredibly tired. So, no, I haven't lost any interest in the things that usually relax me.
Do you feel like you have trouble controlling the worry about your job, or does it feel like something that just naturally takes over your mind, even when you try to resist it?

Control it? Um... no, I wouldn't really say that. I don't think "trouble controlling it" is the right way to describe what's happening, because I'm not actually trying to stop it. 

It's not like it's this chaotic, runaway train that I'm desperately trying to pull the brakes on, and my brain is just rebelling against me. It's really nothing like that. It's more like... I just *am* thinking about it. Because it's important. I mean, if you're looking at a massive portfolio adjustment for a major client, you can't exactly just flip a switch and pretend the risk variables don't exist just because the sun went down. So I don't really try to push the thoughts away or resist them at all. I just follow the problem to its logical conclusion. 

Like, if I wake up at 3 AM, the house is completely quiet, there are no emails coming in, the phone isn't ringing, and my mind just naturally goes to the most pressing thing on my plate, which is always the firm. I don't sit there fighting it or agonizing over the fact that I'm thinking about work. I don't think, "Oh no, here comes the worry, I have to block it out." I just kind of lean into it. I'll just start mentally walking through the spreadsheets. Literally cell by cell, row by row. I'll think about the Q3 projections, and then I'll start calculating how the recent interest rate hikes might affect the debt structuring for this one specific commercial real estate client we have... and I just do it. It’s highly methodical. 

So, no, it definitely doesn't feel like something that takes over my mind against my will. I could probably stop thinking about it if I really, truly wanted to, or if there was an emergency that demanded my immediate attention. It's just that in the middle of the night, there's nothing else to do, and frankly, who else is going to double-check those figures? If I don't run through the models in my head then, I'll just have to do it the second I get to the office anyway. I'm just doing my job in the dark when I should be sleeping. I haven't noticed any feeling of losing control over it, I just... haven't really tried to shut it off.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with persistent, excessive worry focused on specific job-related concerns, accompanied by sleep disturbance and physical symptoms of tension. The worry is not uncontrollable, is circumscribed to occupational matters, and does not generalize to other life domains.
